messages.author: ff1a5632abbf2fe9
messages.subject: factor variable and latent variable interaction in INLA
parts:
Dear INLA experts


My question in general should be called factor latent model interaction. However, to make it concrete, let me give a small example.

I have 30 counties data, and each county is a time series data. Unlike the classical spatial-temporal data structure, the 30 counties are far away from each other, meaning the spatial effect can be neglected. The goal is to study the association between a disease rate with a exposure. To adjust the long term effect, I hope to include a "rw1" latent field and 'iid' latent field for the time for every county. Just like the factor-numeric interaction in R, and the usual code for fixed effect is like

y~ exposure + county/long term function of time

It is unclear how to implement a similar part for the random effect.


Thanks,
Xing

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] factor variable and latent variable interaction in INLA
parts:
1st level: 

y_it ~ Poisson(lamda_it), where  i=1:30, t=1:1000

log(lamda_it)) = beta_0 + beta_1 * x_it + u_it + v_it

2rd level: 
define U_i = {u_i1, u_i2...u_i1000}, V_i = {v_i1, v_i2...v_i1000}

The prior for U_i is 'rw1', and the prior for V_i are 'iid'.
U_i is independent of U_j, when i!=j, similar for V.

Thanks
Xing

>

> define U_i = {u_i1, u_i2...u_i1000}, V_i = {v_i1, v_i2...v_i1000}
>
>
> The prior for U_i is 'rw1', and the prior for V_i are 'iid'.
> U_i is independent of U_j, when i!=j, similar for V.

That would be

formula = y ~ 1 + x + f(time, model="rw1", replicate=i) + f(v,
model="iid")

with appropriate indexes.

check out http://www.r-inla.org/models/tools and option 'replicate'

H

parts:
I checked out the link, getting the definition is: “replicate” generates iid replicates from the same f()-model with the same hyperparameters.
In addition, from the first example(I am not familar with arima.sim), my understanding for the 'same hyperparameters' is as following: all sub-models' hyperpriors  have not only a common distribution, but also identical hyperparameters.
In contrast, a distinct understanding (maybe not your intention) is that all sub-models just share a common hyperprior distribution with different hyperparameters.
What matches the option 'replicate'?

In my application, I think the 2nd would be better, as the 30 counties should present different long-term trend (characterized by the two latent field)

Thanks

parts:
On 20 Feb 2014, at 18:11, Xing Zhao <zhaox...@gmail.com> wrote:
In contrast, a distinct understanding (maybe not your intention) is that all sub-models just share a common hyperprior distribution with different hyperparameters.
What matches the option 'replicate'?

In my application, I think the 2nd would be better, as the 30 counties should present different long-term trend (characterized by the two latent field)

To do that you would need a separate model for each county, which would be computationally expensive due to the large number of parameters, and it is likely that the data doesn't have enough information to identify all those parameters anyway.
But having a common model parameter for all the long-term trends (which is what replicate would do) isn't unreasonable at all as far as I can tell; don't over-complicate your model.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] factor variable and latent variable interaction in INLA
parts:
On Thu, 2014-02-20 at 10:11 -0800, Xing Zhao wrote:
> I checked out the link, getting the definition is: “replicate”
> generates iid replicates from the same f()-model with the same
> hyperparameters.
this is true

> In addition, from the first example(I am not familar with arima.sim),
> my understanding for the 'same hyperparameters' is as following: all
> sub-models' hyperpriors have not only a common distribution, but also
> identical hyperparameters.

f(i, ...), defines a model, x, say with hyperparameters theta.

f(i, ..., replicate = r), defines r replications of x, such that

[x.1, ... , x.r | theta] * [theta] =
[x.1 | theta] * ... * [x.r | theta] [theta]

is their joint distribution. st

Best
